opus-5.5.text:
I don't think of it as choosing one over the others — the idea is that Codex should meet you wherever you already are, and the agent itself is the same underneath. It's really about what kind of work you're doing in that moment.

The terminal is where a lot of us started, and it's great when you want a tight, interactive loop: you're in your repo, you want to ask Codex to poke around, run some commands, fix a failing test, and you're watching it closely and steering. It feels very natural for engineers who live in the command line.

The IDE extension is for when you're deep in the code yourself. You've got files open, you're reading and editing, and you want Codex right next to you with that context: "refactor this function," "explain what's going on here," "write tests for this module." It's pairing, basically, where you stay very hands-on.

And then GitHub and the cloud side is where delegation really shines. You can kick off a bunch of tasks in parallel, let them run in their own sandboxed environments, and come back to review the results as pull requests. Code review is also a big one there. Having Codex review PRs has become something a lot of teams at OpenAI rely on, because it catches real bugs before they get merged.

So the way I'd put it: terminal and IDE for when you're working synchronously alongside the agent, and GitHub and the cloud for when you want to hand off work and fan it out. What we've seen is that people mix all three. You might start something locally, push it to the cloud to keep going while you're in a meeting, and then review it on GitHub. The goal is for that to feel seamless, so the context follows you rather than you having to think about which surface you're on.

r001.rationale: The response describes the terminal as useful for an interactive loop, but does not say power users tend to use it for more complex workflows.

r002.rationale: It links IDE use to having files open and working hands-on, but does not connect that preference to seeing code changes.

r003.rationale: The response says terminal users watch Codex closely and steer it; it does not characterize vibe coding as prioritizing the outcome over attention to generated code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on where you are in the work, and I actually don't think of them as competing options so much as different surfaces for the same agent.

The way I'd frame it: the terminal is where I go when I'm in the flow of building something and I want to be very close to the agent. I can see what it's doing, I can interrupt it, I can steer it. It's very tactile. When I'm iterating quickly, when I'm not totally sure what the right approach is, when I want to be in a conversation with the model, the terminal is great for that. It's fast and it fits into whatever workflow you already have.

The IDE is more about when you're already in the code, you're reading it, you're editing it yourself, and you want Codex right there alongside you. You can highlight something, ask a question, have it make a change, and you see the diff immediately in the environment you're already looking at. It's more of a collaborative editing mode. The context switching cost is very low because you never leave the editor.

And then GitHub is really about delegation. That's the one where I'm not sitting there watching. I have a task that's well-scoped enough that I can hand it off, go do something else, and come back to a pull request. Fix this bug, add tests for this module, address the review comments on this PR. That's where you really start to get the leverage of running many things in parallel, because the agent is working in its own environment and you're just reviewing the output.

So the mental model I'd give people is: how much do you want to be in the loop right now? If the answer is "a lot," terminal or IDE. If the answer is "I trust this task is clear and I just want the result," hand it off through GitHub. And a lot of the work we're doing is about making it seamless to move between those modes, so you can start something in the terminal, realize it's bigger than you thought, and kick it off to run in the background, or start something in the cloud and pull it down locally to finish it. The goal is that it should feel like one Codex that you're just interacting with from wherever is most convenient.

r001.rationale: The response describes using the terminal for fast iteration and uncertain work, but does not say power users tend to use it for more complex Codex workflows.

r002.rationale: It says the IDE shows the diff immediately in the environment where the user is already working, linking IDE use to seeing code changes.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize terminal vibe coding as focusing on the desired outcome over reviewing generated code; it instead emphasizes seeing, interrupting, and steering the agent.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of where you are in the workflow and how closely you want to collaborate with the agent. If you’re in the IDE, you’re looking at code, you have context in front of you, and you probably want that tight loop: ask for a change, inspect it, iterate. The terminal is a natural fit if that’s already where you work—you’re running commands, testing things, moving between tools.

GitHub is more useful when the task is something you can hand off. You can describe what you want, let the agent work on it, and come back to review the proposed change.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing one interface forever. You might start with a task in GitHub, then pull it into your IDE or terminal to work through the details. The interface should fit the way you want to work at that moment.

r001.rationale: It says the terminal suits people who already work there and run commands, but does not say power users tend to use it for more complex workflows.

r002.rationale: It links IDE use to having code context in front of you and being able to inspect proposed changes in a tight iteration loop.

r003.rationale: It does not describe terminal-based vibe coding as focusing on the desired outcome rather than attending to generated code.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on where you are in the work. If you have a well-defined task you can hand off and come back to review, GitHub is a natural place for that. If you’re actively exploring the code and making decisions as you go, the IDE gives you that tight interaction. And if you already spend a lot of time in the terminal, it makes sense to work with Codex there.

I wouldn’t think of those as three competing choices. You might start with a task in GitHub, then move into the IDE or terminal to work through the details. The important thing is that you can use it where you’re comfortable and choose how involved you want to be at that moment.

r002.rationale: It describes the IDE as useful for active exploration and decisions, but does not connect IDE preference to seeing code changes.
